name: ARTAS robotic system

lead: ARTAS is a robot from Restoration Robotics that finds and extracts donor hair follicles during FUE hair transplants, which restore density to the hairline and crown. It was reported cleared by the FDA in 2011 for harvesting hair in men with androgenetic alopecia.

Imaging maps the donor scalp and a dual-needle punch extracts follicular units. It automates harvesting only, and implantation still involves the surgical team. Registered manufacturer-associated trials compare it with manual harvest, but no results were available in the sources reviewed.

paras: The surgical team uses the robot for the extraction step of an FUE session, then implants the grafts. Operators need training, and it is offered by clinics that own the system.
Risks are those of FUE generally. Reference sources note higher cost than manual FUE, limits to FUE-style harvesting and the need for trained operators.

chain: Grafts are transplanted to thin areas
angle.text: ARTAS is an FDA-cleared image-guided robot that automates donor hair extraction in FUE transplants, which restore visible density to the hairline and crown. Published outcome data comparing it with manual harvest are thin.

lead: The ARTAS system is a computer-assisted robotic device for hair restoration, made by Restoration Robotics and now marketed by Venus Concept. It uses image guidance to identify and extract individual follicular units from the donor scalp in follicular unit extraction (FUE), the technique that leaves small dot-like scars rather than a linear strip scar.[1][2][3]

People pursue it to restore hair density and a lower, fuller hairline: donor hairs taken from the back and sides of the scalp are moved to thinning areas, and transplanted hair is described as donor-dominant, meaning it keeps growing as it would have at its original site.[1] The robot automates the extraction step, which surgeons otherwise perform by hand with small punches.

Reference sources report US FDA clearance in 2011 for harvesting hair in men with brown or black hair, and describe a system using high-definition imaging and a dual-needle punch.[1][2] Reported drawbacks include higher cost than manual FUE, limits to FUE-style harvesting and the need for trained operators.[2] ClinicalTrials.gov lists manufacturer-associated studies comparing computer-assisted and manual harvest, but no results have been published.[4][5][6]
infobox: 2011, for harvesting in men with brown or black hair[1]
Not given; transplants are priced per graft, from about US$1.07 in Turkey to US$7.00 in Canada[1]

paras: According to a general reference, cameras map the donor area, and a dual-needle punch extracts follicular units; the cited punch depth is about 1 mm and the article cites transection rates under 5 percent and 400 to 800 grafts per hour.[2] Those numbers come from a reference page, not from trial data.

The manufacturer describes its current ARTAS iXi model as using a multi-camera stereoscopic vision system with stated 44-micron resolution, a seven-axis robotic arm and a proprietary punch, with touchscreen planning for the recipient area and the ability to create recipient sites and implant grafts in one platform; these are company claims.[3] The company also cites a 91 percent 'Worth It' rating on a patient review platform and states Health Canada licensing for harvesting follicles in men with black or brown straight hair.[3]

FUE generally uses 0.6 to 1.0 mm punches under local anaesthesia, takes under a week to recover from, needs no suture removal, and is described as longer and more costly than strip harvesting; Wikipedia notes patient candidacy is restricted.[1]

Wikipedia states the ARTAS system was approved by the FDA in 2011 for harvesting follicular units from men with brown or black hair.[1] Grokipedia describes the clearance as a 510(k) for men with androgenetic alopecia.[2]

Earlier milestones include Norman Orentreich's late-1950s work demonstrating donor dominance, and strip excision and stereo-microscopic dissection in the 1980s; NeoGraft received FDA approval in 2009 before ARTAS in 2011.[1]

Hair-loss discussion on T Nation has included the claim that the ARTAS machine has made hair transplantation easier, quicker and nearly undetectable, with a link to the manufacturer's product page.[7] Per Wikipedia's hair-transplantation history, techniques progressed from plugs and strip excision in the 20th century to follicular unit grafts, and robotic devices arrived after 2009.[1] Cost in the US, UK and Turkey varies widely by clinic and number of grafts.[1]

Grokipedia lists costs 20 to 40 percent above manual FUE and the need for specialised training.[2] A Canadian aesthetic surgery meeting abstract argued that most hair restoration candidates are not appropriate for FUE whether manual, NeoGraft-assisted or ARTAS robotic.

No results have been published. Registered studies include a 2009 comparison of computer-assisted versus manual hair harvest (n=37),[4] a 2016 comparison of computer-assisted and manual implantation (n=32)[5] and a larger registered computer-assisted restoration study (n=150).[6]

lore.intro: On forums, ARTAS is mentioned as technology that makes hair transplants more precise and less visible.[7]

claims.claim: Robotic FUE makes transplants nearly undetectable
Robotic harvesting is more consistent than a human hand

timeline.event: Norman Orentreich transplants donor grafts for male pattern baldness and shows donor dominance.[1]
NeoGraft becomes the first FDA-approved robotic hair restoration device.[1]
FDA clearance of the ARTAS system for FUE harvesting.[1][2]
Registered studies of computer-assisted implantation begin.[5][6]
